newsitem.title: CANADA: CAW tells members to okay Canadian Airlines deal.
newsitem.headline: CAW tells members to okay Canadian Airlines deal.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers, the final union to capitulate to troubled Canadian Airlines Corp's restructuring package, recommended to its members on Saturday that they accept the company's offer.
A ratification vote on the deal will begin on Wednesday across the country, Anne Davidson, president of local 1990 of the CAW told reporters at a news conference.
The union agreed to wage cuts of about 3.7 percent over the four-year deal, as well as several other concessions in exchange for job security for some of its members.

They also won the airline's agreement to pay all laid-off workers 40 weeks salary in compensation and, when it eventually returns to profitability, to set up a pool of its profits to give workers a cost of living allowance.

Davidson said the structure of the wage cut was designed to protect low-income earners, and there would be no cuts in annual salaries of up to C$25,000 ($18,409). All gross salaries above that amount will be cut by 10 percent.
The CAW, which represents ticket agents, fought the deal for five weeks. It was the last of six unions to agree to Canadian's plan.
Canadian sought wage reductions of C$35 million ($26 million) a year from its 16,500 employees, saying the cuts were crucial to the company's survival.
The union finally reached a deal with the airline Friday but only on the condition that the federal government agree to a review of airline industry regulations.

"In the early hours of this morning, we finally agreed on the language of a letter from the government (promising to establish a committee to consider the future of the airline industry," Davidson said.
The union and the Ministry of Transport haggled over the language of the letter for a day and a half, a struggle that the CAW's Basil Hargrove said the union won.

According to a letter signed by Transport Minister David Anderson, a government-established committee -- made up of the unions, air carriers, consumer groups, airline industry analysts and others -- will review the state of the industry, and recommend steps to improve stability and competitiveness.

The Canadian restructuring plan also includes federal and provincial government support and a C$48 million ($36 million) yearly cut in fees paid to the airline's 33 percent-owner AMR Corp, the parent of American Airlines.
Canadian is also trying to postpone about C$170 million ($125 million) in debt payments over the next six months, a move contingent on the plan being in place.
